purpose: Recent empirical evidence for the Session 3 labor-market sequence. Publication dates and observation periods are distinguished on the slides.

job_polarization.status: Restored existing vector figure without changing the historical series or its established four-group construction.
job_polarization.source: BLS Current Population Survey, via FRED. The chart is descriptive historical context, not a causal AI estimate.
job_polarization.interpretation: Broad occupational proxies, not a task-level classification of every job. Indexed employment levels, not employment shares or wages.

workplace_productivity.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey Raymond
workplace_productivity.title: Generative AI at Work
workplace_productivity.evidence: Abstract, Introduction and Table II. 5,172 customer-support agents; staggered deployment mainly fall 2020 and winter 2021; issues resolved per hour increase about 15% on average.
workplace_productivity.scope: One Fortune 500 business-software firm and its subcontractors. Most agents located outside the US. Larger gains for less experienced and lower-skill agents.
workplace_productivity.limits: Staggered rollout study, not a general estimate of AI effects on employment or wages. Do not relabel 2020–2021 data as post-ChatGPT evidence.

denmark.title: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI
denmark.version: March 13, 2026; previously circulated as Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects
denmark.evidence: Abstract and Section 3. Administrative records through December 2024 linked to adoption surveys. Difference-in-differences estimates find no detectable effects on earnings or recorded hours, ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT launch.
denmark.limits: The 2% bound concerns earnings and recorded hours; it is not a bound for every occupation-specific employment estimate. New AI tasks and work reorganization are documented despite small average effects.

young_us_workers.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, Ruyu Chen
young_us_workers.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
young_us_workers.evidence: Abstract and Sections 2.2–2.4. ADP sample through June 2026. For ages 22–25, employment in the top two AI-exposure quintiles is 19% below a counterfactual keeping pace with the bottom three quintiles since November 2022; adjustment mainly via reduced hiring.
young_us_workers.limits: 19% is a relative kept-pace shortfall, not the absolute employment decline, percentage-point change or a causal AI estimate. Experienced workers show no comparable exposure gap; pretrends and sample representativeness remain concerns.
